questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Polygenic inheritance with three additive genes: number of phenotypic classes and frequency of the middle class
questions.question: Skin colour in a model organism is controlled by three unlinked genes A, B and C. Each capital allele adds one equal unit of pigment, and small alleles add none. Two individuals with genotype AaBbCc are crossed. How many phenotypic classes appear among the offspring, and what fraction of the offspring has exactly three capital alleles?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 7 classes; 5/16.
Concept: In polygenic inheritance, a trait is controlled by several genes, and the phenotype reflects the total contribution of all the alleles (additive effect). Individuals with the same number of capital alleles have the same phenotype, whatever the genes carrying them.
Given: parents AaBbCc × AaBbCc; three unlinked genes; each capital allele adds one unit.
Formula/Principle: each offspring receives 6 alleles, each capital with probability 1/2; P(k capital alleles) = C(6, k)/2⁶.
Step 1: The number of capital alleles can be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6, so there are 7 phenotypic classes.
Step 2: P(3 capital alleles) = C(6, 3)/64 = 20/64 = 5/16.
Why: The classes follow the binomial coefficients 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1 out of 64. The middle class (three capital alleles, the same as the parents) is the commonest, which gives the bell-shaped distribution typical of polygenic traits.
Why not the others: (A) 8 counts the combinations of three genes as dominant or recessive (2³), which applies only with complete dominance; 1/8 is not any class frequency. (B) 27 is the number of genotypes (3³), not phenotypes, and 1/64 is the frequency of an extreme class. (C) The number of classes is right, but 1/64 is the frequency of the darkest (or lightest) class only.
Key point: n additive genes → 2n + 1 phenotypic classes in the ratio of binomial coefficients.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Time for replication of the E. coli chromosome with two forks, and number of Okazaki fragments
questions.question: The chromosome of Escherichia coli has \(4.6\times10^6\) base pairs and one origin of replication. Replication proceeds in both directions from the origin, and each replication fork moves at 1000 nucleotides per second along each template. On the lagging strand, DNA is made as Okazaki fragments of about 1000 nucleotides each. About how long does one round of replication take, and about how many Okazaki fragments are made in all?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 38 minutes; about 4600 fragments.
Concept: Replication starts at the origin and forms a replication fork moving in each direction. DNA polymerase works only in the 5′ → 3′ direction, so at each fork one strand is made continuously (leading strand) and the other discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments (lagging strand), which are joined by DNA ligase.
Given: genome = 4.6 × 10⁶ bp; 2 forks; 1000 nucleotides per second per fork; Okazaki fragment ≈ 1000 nucleotides.
Formula/Principle: each fork copies half of the chromosome; time = (length per fork) ÷ (rate); lagging-strand length = whole genome (half at each fork).
Step 1: Each fork copies 2.3 × 10⁶ bp, so time = 2.3 × 10⁶ ÷ 1000 = 2300 s ≈ 38 minutes.
Step 2: At each fork the lagging strand is 2.3 × 10⁶ nucleotides, giving 2300 fragments; two forks give about 4600 fragments.
Why: The two forks work at the same time, so they share the chromosome. Only one of the two new strands at each fork is lagging, so the total length made as fragments equals one genome length.
Why not the others: (A) 77 minutes assumes a single fork copying the whole chromosome. (C) 9200 counts both new strands as discontinuous; the leading strand is made continuously. (D) 19 minutes takes 2000 nucleotides per second per fork, and 2300 counts the fragments at one fork only.
Key point: Bidirectional replication halves the time; only the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Yield of ethanol and carbon dioxide in alcoholic fermentation by yeast
questions.question: In making an alcoholic beverage, Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments glucose by the overall reaction \(\ce{C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2}\). If 90 g of glucose is completely fermented, what masses of ethanol and carbon dioxide are formed? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
options: A) 46 g of ethanol and 44 g of carbon dioxide
B) 92 g of ethanol and 88 g of carbon dioxide
C) 23 g of ethanol and 22 g of carbon dioxide
D) 46 g of ethanol and 22 g of carbon dioxide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 46 g of ethanol and 44 g of carbon dioxide.
Concept: Brewer's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide; this is used to make wine, beer and other alcoholic drinks. One glucose molecule gives two ethanol and two carbon dioxide molecules.
Given: 90 g glucose; M(glucose) = 180 g mol⁻¹, M(ethanol) = 46 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44 g mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: moles = mass ÷ molar mass; 1 mol glucose → 2 mol ethanol + 2 mol CO₂.
Step 1: Glucose = 90 ÷ 180 = 0.50 mol.
Step 2: Ethanol = 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 mol = 46 g; CO₂ = 1.0 mol = 44 g.
Why: Check: 46 + 44 = 90 g, equal to the mass of glucose used, as conservation of mass requires.
Why not the others: (B) It treats 90 g as 1 mol of glucose; the total 180 g would be twice the mass used. (C) It takes one ethanol and one CO₂ per glucose. (D) Ethanol and CO₂ are formed in equal numbers of moles, so their masses must be 46 g and 44 g, not 46 g and 22 g.
Key point: 1 glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂; mass is conserved.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Making E. coli competent with calcium ions and heat shock
questions.question: Escherichia coli cells are mixed with a plasmid that carries an ampicillin-resistance gene and spread on ampicillin plates. In batch P, the cells were first treated with cold calcium chloride solution, kept on ice with the plasmid, given a brief heat shock at 42 °C and returned to ice. Batch Q was treated in the same way except that calcium chloride was left out. Many colonies grow from P but almost none from Q. What is the best interpretation?
options: A) Calcium ions supply energy for replicating the plasmid inside the cell
B) Calcium ions inactivate ampicillin in the plate, so more cells survive in P
C) Treating cells with a divalent cation such as calcium makes them competent, raising the chance that DNA enters through the cell wall and membrane during the heat shock
D) The heat shock alone is enough for uptake of DNA, so the difference must be due to contamination
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Treating cells with a divalent cation such as calcium makes them competent, raising the chance that DNA enters through the cell wall and membrane during the heat shock.
Concept: DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass easily through cell membranes. To take up a plasmid, bacterial cells must be made competent. This is done by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium, then incubating with the DNA on ice, giving a brief heat shock at 42 °C, and putting them back on ice.
Why: Only P was treated with calcium, and only P gave many ampicillin-resistant colonies. The difference shows that the calcium treatment is what allowed the plasmid to enter. The resistant colonies are cells that took up the plasmid.
Why not the others: (A) Calcium does not power plasmid replication; replication uses the host cell's machinery. (B) The calcium is applied to the cells before plating, not to destroy ampicillin; untransformed cells still die on the plate. (D) Q also received the heat shock and gave almost no colonies, so the heat shock alone is not enough.
Key point: Competence = divalent cation treatment + ice + heat shock (42 °C) + ice.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Telling mutualism from commensalism in four pairs of organisms
questions.question:
Which statement correctly classifies all four interactions?
(i) An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch
(ii) A fungus and a photosynthesising alga forming a lichen
(iii) Barnacles growing on the back of a whale
(iv) A fig species and the wasp species that pollinates it while laying eggs in its fruit
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (i) commensalism, (ii) mutualism, (iii) commensalism, (iv) mutualism.
Concept: In commensalism one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor helped (+/0). In mutualism both species benefit (+/+). In parasitism one benefits and the other is harmed (+/−).
Why: (i) The orchid gets support and light; the mango tree gains nothing and loses nothing: commensalism. (ii) The fungus gets food from the alga, and the alga gets shelter and absorbed water and minerals from the fungus: mutualism. (iii) Barnacles get a surface and transport; the whale is not affected: commensalism. (iv) The fig is pollinated, and the wasp gets a safe site for its eggs and food for its larvae: mutualism.
Why not the others: (A) The mango tree gains nothing from the orchid, and the fungus and alga both benefit in a lichen. (C) The orchid takes no food from the mango, barnacles do not harm the whale, and the fig–wasp pair is mutualism. (D) The whale gains nothing from barnacles, and fig and wasp help each other rather than compete.
Key point: Mutualism +/+; commensalism +/0; parasitism +/−.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Net primary productivity of land and ocean per unit area
questions.question: Of the annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere, about 170 billion tonnes (dry weight), the oceans produce only about 55 billion tonnes, although they cover about 70% of the Earth's surface. Taking these figures, how does the net primary productivity per unit area of land compare with that of the oceans, and what is the main reason?
options: A) About equal, because both receive about the same sunlight per unit area
B) The ocean is about twice as productive per unit area, because water is never limiting there
C) Land is about 2 times as productive per unit area, because land plants are larger
D) Land is about 5 times as productive per unit area, mainly because productivity in the open ocean is limited by low supply of mineral nutrients and by light reaching only the surface layer
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Land is about 5 times as productive per unit area, mainly because productivity in the open ocean is limited by low supply of mineral nutrients and by light reaching only the surface layer.
Concept: Primary productivity depends on the plant species, environmental factors, the availability of nutrients and the photosynthetic capacity of plants. Net primary productivity (NPP) is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs.
Given: total NPP = 170; ocean NPP = 55, so land NPP = 115 (billion tonnes per year); ocean area = 70%, land area = 30%.
Formula/Principle: productivity per unit area ∝ (NPP of that part) ÷ (its share of area).
Step 1: Land: 115 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 383; ocean: 55 ÷ 0.70 ≈ 79 (same arbitrary units).
Step 2: Ratio = 383 ÷ 79 ≈ 4.9, so about 5 times.
Why: Much of the open ocean is poor in mineral nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, and light reaches only the upper layer of water. So, although the ocean is vast, its productivity per unit area is low.
Why not the others: (A) The ratio is about 5, not 1; sunlight is not the only factor. (B) Water is plentiful in the ocean, but nutrients, not water, limit productivity there. (C) The ratio is about 5, and plant size does not set productivity per unit area.
Key point: Ocean NPP is low per unit area because of nutrient limitation, despite its large area.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Biodiversity and ecosystem stability: interpreting a long-term plot experiment
questions.question: In a long-term field experiment, grassland plots were sown with different numbers of plant species and watched for many years. Plots with more species showed less variation in total plant biomass from year to year, and also produced more biomass on average. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A) Communities with more species tend to be more stable and more productive
B) Species richness has no effect on how an ecosystem functions
C) Plots with fewer species are more stable because they suffer less competition
D) Stability depends only on rainfall, not on the number of species
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Communities with more species tend to be more stable and more productive.
Concept: A stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, should resist occasional disturbance, and should resist invasion by alien species. Long-term outdoor plot experiments showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.
Why: The plots differ in the number of species, and the plots with more species varied less and produced more. This supports the idea that biodiversity is essential for ecosystem health and that losing species can harm ecosystem function, as suggested by the rivet popper hypothesis.
Why not the others: (B) The results show clear differences linked to species number. (C) The observed pattern is the opposite: plots with fewer species varied more. (D) All plots shared the same weather, so rainfall cannot explain the difference between them.
Key point: More species → less year-to-year variation and higher productivity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Five-kingdom classification from cell type, wall, nutrition and body organisation
questions.question:
The table describes four organisms.

Organism | Cell type | Cell wall | Body | Nutrition
P | prokaryotic | peptidoglycan | unicellular | photosynthetic
Q | eukaryotic | none; flexible pellicle | unicellular | photosynthetic in light, heterotrophic in the dark
R | eukaryotic | chitin | unicellular | absorbs dissolved food; reproduces by budding
S | eukaryotic | cellulose | multicellular with tissues | photosynthetic

In Whittaker's five-kingdom system, which assignment is correct?
options: A) P Monera, Q Plantae, R Protista, S Plantae
B) P Protista, Q Protista, R Fungi, S Plantae
C) P Monera, Q Protista, R Fungi, S Plantae
D) P Monera, Q Protista, R Protista, S Plantae
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P Monera, Q Protista, R Fungi, S Plantae.
Concept: Whittaker used cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Monera are prokaryotes. Protista are unicellular eukaryotes. Fungi are heterotrophs with a chitin wall that absorb food (saprophytes); most are multicellular, but yeast is unicellular. Plantae are multicellular eukaryotic autotrophs with cellulose walls.
Why: P is prokaryotic, so it is in Monera (like cyanobacteria). Q is a unicellular eukaryote with a pellicle that can switch between photosynthesis and heterotrophy, like Euglena: Protista. R has a chitin wall, absorbs food and buds, like yeast: Fungi, even though it is unicellular. S is a multicellular photosynthetic eukaryote with a cellulose wall: Plantae.
Why not the others: (A) Q has no cell wall and is unicellular, so it is not a plant; R has a chitin wall, which places it in Fungi. (B) P is prokaryotic and belongs to Monera, not Protista. (D) A chitin wall and absorptive nutrition place R in Fungi; being unicellular does not make it a protist.
Key point: Chitin wall + absorptive nutrition = Fungi, whether unicellular (yeast) or multicellular.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why red algae can live at greater depths than green algae
questions.question: In a clear sea, divers find that green algae are common near the surface, while red algae are common at much greater depths. Water absorbs red light within the first few metres, while blue-green light penetrates much deeper. Which explanation fits the observation?
options: A) Red algae have no chlorophyll, so they do not need light
B) Red algae are heterotrophic and feed on organic matter that sinks
C) Green algae are poisoned by the higher pressure at depth
D) Red algae have the pigment r-phycoerythrin, which absorbs the blue-green light that reaches great depths and passes the energy to chlorophyll
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Red algae have the pigment r-phycoerythrin, which absorbs the blue-green light that reaches great depths and passes the energy to chlorophyll.
Concept: Algae are grouped into Chlorophyceae (green), Phaeophyceae (brown) and Rhodophyceae (red). Red algae owe their colour to r-phycoerythrin. Most are marine, and many live at great depths in the sea, where little light penetrates.
Why: At depth only blue-green light is left. Phycoerythrin absorbs this light well, so red algae can still photosynthesise there. Green algae depend mainly on chlorophylls a and b, which absorb red and blue light, and red light is absent at depth.
Why not the others: (A) Red algae do have chlorophyll a; phycoerythrin is an accessory pigment that adds to it. (B) Red algae are photosynthetic autotrophs. (C) The distribution matches the light available; pressure is not the explanation.
Key point: Phycoerythrin lets red algae use the blue-green light that reaches deep water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Storage roots: modified tap root and modified adventitious root
questions.question: The carrot and the sweet potato both store food in swollen roots. How do these two storage organs compare?
options: A) Both store food, but the carrot is a modified tap root while the sweet potato is a modified adventitious root
B) Both are modified stems, because they store food underground
C) The carrot is a modified adventitious root and the sweet potato a modified tap root
D) Both are modified tap roots, because both grow downwards into the soil
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both store food, but the carrot is a modified tap root while the sweet potato is a modified adventitious root.
Concept: Roots are modified for storage, support or respiration. The tap root of carrot, turnip and radish swells to store food. In the sweet potato, adventitious roots (roots that arise from parts other than the radicle) swell to store food.
Why: The carrot develops from the radicle as a single main root that swells. The sweet potato forms many swollen roots from the nodes of its creeping stem, so they are adventitious roots. The function is the same, but the origin differs.
Why not the others: (B) Both are roots: they have no nodes, internodes or buds, unlike the stem tuber of potato. (C) It swaps the two origins. (D) The swollen roots of sweet potato arise from the stem, so they are adventitious, not tap roots.
Key point: Carrot = tap root; sweet potato = adventitious root; potato = stem tuber.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Telling dicot and monocot roots apart by the number of xylem bundles and the pith
questions.question: The figure shows transverse sections of two young roots, X and Y, with the xylem and phloem patches labelled. Count the patches in the figure. Which statement is correct?
options: A) X is a monocot root and Y a dicot root; together they have 9 phloem patches
B) X is a dicot root and Y a monocot root; together they have 9 phloem patches
C) X is a dicot root and Y a monocot root; together they have 18 phloem patches
D) Both are dicot roots; together they have 18 phloem patches
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X is a dicot root and Y a monocot root; together they have 18 phloem patches.
Concept: In roots the vascular bundles are radial: xylem and phloem lie in separate patches on different radii and alternate with each other, so their numbers are equal. A dicot root usually has two to four xylem patches and little or no pith. A monocot root has more than six xylem patches (polyarch) and a large, well-developed pith.
Given: from the figure, X has 4 xylem patches and no pith; Y has 14 xylem patches and a large pith.
Formula/Principle: in a radial arrangement, number of phloem patches = number of xylem patches.
Step 1: X: 4 xylem patches (tetrarch), no pith → dicot root, with 4 phloem patches.
Step 2: Y: 14 xylem patches (polyarch), large pith → monocot root, with 14 phloem patches. Total = 4 + 14 = 18.
Why: The number of xylem patches and the size of the pith are the standard features for telling the two root types apart.
Why not the others: (A) It swaps the roots: polyarch with a large pith is the monocot. (B) The identities are right, but 9 halves the count; each xylem patch has a matching phloem patch. (D) Fourteen xylem patches and a large pith are features of a monocot root.
Key point: Dicot root: 2–4 xylem, little pith; monocot root: polyarch, large pith; xylem and phloem patches are equal in number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Relative gut length of the herbivorous tadpole and the carnivorous adult frog
questions.question: A tadpole of body length 4 cm has a coiled intestine 30 cm long. The adult frog of body length 8 cm has an intestine 12 cm long. By how many times is the gut length relative to body length greater in the tadpole than in the adult, and what explains the difference?
options: A) 2.5 times, because the adult has stopped growing
B) 5 times, because the tadpole feeds on plant material, which needs a long gut for digestion, while the adult is carnivorous and has a short gut
C) 5 times, because the adult absorbs most food through its skin
D) 0.2 times, because the adult needs a longer gut for its larger body
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5 times, because the tadpole feeds on plant material, which needs a long gut for digestion, while the adult is carnivorous and has a short gut.
Concept: The alimentary canal of the adult frog is short because frogs are carnivores, and the length of the intestine is reduced. Herbivores have long guts because plant food is slow to digest. The frog tadpole is mainly herbivorous.
Given: tadpole: body 4 cm, gut 30 cm; adult: body 8 cm, gut 12 cm.
Formula/Principle: relative gut length = gut length ÷ body length; compare the two ratios.
Step 1: Tadpole: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5; adult: 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5.
Step 2: 7.5 ÷ 1.5 = 5.
Why: During metamorphosis the diet changes from plant matter to insects and other animals, and the gut shortens to suit a diet that is digested quickly.
Why not the others: (A) 2.5 compares the gut lengths (30 ÷ 12) without allowing for body size. (C) Food is not absorbed through the skin; the skin is used for respiration. (D) 0.2 is the inverse ratio; the adult's relative gut length is smaller, not larger.
Key point: Herbivore → long gut; carnivore → short gut.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Abundance of smooth and rough endoplasmic reticulum in cells that secrete lipids and proteins
questions.question: Electron micrographs of two kinds of animal cells are compared. Cell X has an extensive network of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) and little rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). Cell Y is packed with RER and has a large Golgi apparatus. What do these observations suggest about the main products of the two cells?
options: A) X mainly makes lipid-like steroid hormones, while Y mainly makes and secretes proteins
B) X mainly makes and secretes proteins, while Y mainly makes steroid hormones
C) Both cells mainly store starch, which is made on the endoplasmic reticulum
D) X mainly digests worn-out organelles, while Y mainly makes ATP
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X mainly makes lipid-like steroid hormones, while Y mainly makes and secretes proteins.
Concept: Rough ER carries ribosomes and is active in protein synthesis and secretion. Smooth ER is the major site for synthesis of lipids; in animal cells, lipid-like steroidal hormones are made in the SER. The Golgi apparatus packages materials and is especially well developed in secretory cells.
Why: An extensive SER points to a lipid-making cell, such as a cell that secretes steroid hormones. A cell packed with RER and with a large Golgi apparatus is specialised for making and packaging secretory proteins, such as an enzyme-secreting gland cell.
Why not the others: (B) It swaps the roles: ribosomes, and so protein synthesis, are on the RER of cell Y. (C) Animal cells do not store starch, and starch is not made on the ER. (D) Digestion of worn-out organelles is the job of lysosomes, and ATP is made mainly in mitochondria.
Key point: SER → lipids and steroid hormones; RER + Golgi → secretory proteins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Estimating the duration of mitosis and of metaphase from counts in an onion root tip
questions.question:
In a squash of an onion root tip, 1000 cells were classified as follows.

Stage | Interphase | Prophase | Metaphase | Anaphase | Telophase
Number of cells | 880 | 70 | 20 | 15 | 15

The cells divide asynchronously, and the whole cell cycle takes 24 hours. The time spent in a stage is proportional to the fraction of cells seen in it. About how long do mitosis (M phase) and metaphase last?
options: A) M phase about 12 minutes; metaphase about 29 minutes
B) M phase about 21 hours; metaphase about 29 minutes
C) M phase about 2.9 hours; metaphase about 2 minutes
D) M phase about 2.9 hours; metaphase about 29 minutes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) M phase about 2.9 hours; metaphase about 29 minutes.
Concept: The cell cycle has an interphase (G₁, S, G₂), which takes most of the time, and a short M phase made of prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. In an asynchronous population, the fraction of cells in a stage equals the fraction of the cycle spent in it.
Why: Cells in M phase = 70 + 20 + 15 + 15 = 120, so M phase = 120/1000 × 24 h = 2.88 h ≈ 2.9 h. Metaphase = 20/1000 × 24 h = 0.48 h ≈ 29 minutes. Interphase takes 880/1000 × 24 = 21.1 h, which is the larger part of the cycle, as expected.
Why not the others: (A) 12 minutes takes 120 out of 1000 as minutes, not as a fraction of 24 hours. (B) About 21 hours is the length of interphase, not of M phase. (C) M phase is right, but 2 minutes uses the count of 20 as if it were 2 out of 1000.
Key point: Duration of a stage = (cells in that stage ÷ total cells) × length of the cycle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Chemiosmosis when the ATP synthase of the thylakoid is destroyed
questions.question: In illuminated chloroplasts, a chemical destroys the ATP synthase (CF₀–CF₁) of the thylakoid membrane but leaves the electron transport chain and the membrane itself intact. What happens?
options: A) No proton gradient forms, because protons are pumped by the ATP synthase
B) ATP is still made at the same rate, because ATP is formed by the electron carriers themselves
C) Protons still build up in the lumen, but ATP is not made, so the Calvin cycle slows for lack of ATP
D) NADPH formation stops at once, because NADPH is made by the ATP synthase
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Protons still build up in the lumen, but ATP is not made, so the Calvin cycle slows for lack of ATP.
Concept: In chemiosmosis, electron transport and the splitting of water build up protons inside the thylakoid lumen. The protons flow back to the stroma through the CF₀ channel of the ATP synthase, and this flow drives the CF₁ part to make ATP. The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses ATP and NADPH.
Why: Electron transport still pumps protons into the lumen, so the gradient forms. With no ATP synthase, protons cannot flow back through it, so no ATP is made. Without ATP the Calvin cycle cannot continue for long.
Why not the others: (A) Protons are moved into the lumen by the electron transport chain and water splitting, not by the ATP synthase. (B) ATP is made by the ATP synthase using the proton flow, not by the electron carriers. (D) NADPH is made by NADP reductase at the end of the electron chain, not by the ATP synthase.
Key point: Electron transport makes the proton gradient; ATP synthase uses it to make ATP.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Need to regenerate oxaloacetate for the citric acid cycle to continue
questions.question: In a cell, much of the oxaloacetate of the mitochondria is drawn off to make amino acids and is not replaced from other sources. Acetyl CoA is still supplied normally. Why does the activity of the citric acid (TCA) cycle fall?
options: A) Oxaloacetate is the source of the acetyl group that is oxidised in the cycle
B) Oxaloacetate is needed to combine with acetyl CoA to form citric acid, and it is regenerated only by the cycle itself
C) Oxaloacetate is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain
D) Oxaloacetate is needed to convert glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Oxaloacetate is needed to combine with acetyl CoA to form citric acid, and it is regenerated only by the cycle itself.
Concept: The TCA cycle starts when the acetyl group of acetyl CoA condenses with oxaloacetic acid (OAA) and water to form citric acid. The cycle then oxidises citrate in steps and finally regenerates OAA, so the cycle continues as long as OAA is regenerated and acetyl CoA is supplied.
Why: If OAA is taken away faster than it is regenerated, less is available to accept acetyl groups. Acetyl CoA cannot enter the cycle without OAA, so less citrate forms and the whole cycle slows, even though acetyl CoA is plentiful.
Why not the others: (A) The acetyl group comes from acetyl CoA, not from OAA. (C) The final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain is oxygen. (D) Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and does not need OAA.
Key point: OAA + acetyl CoA → citrate; OAA must be regenerated for the cycle to turn.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Role of bile in fat digestion: effect of a blocked bile duct
questions.question: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct of a patient. Pancreatic juice still reaches the duodenum. The patient's faeces now contain much undigested fat. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Bile contains lipase, the main fat-digesting enzyme, which can no longer reach the gut
B) Bile is needed to activate trypsinogen, which digests fats
C) Without bile the stomach cannot secrete gastric lipase
D) Bile salts break fat into very small droplets (emulsification), which gives lipase a much larger surface to act on; without bile, fat digestion and absorption are poor
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Bile salts break fat into very small droplets (emulsification), which gives lipase a much larger surface to act on; without bile, fat digestion and absorption are poor.
Concept: Bile released into the duodenum contains bile pigments, bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids, but no enzymes. Bile helps in emulsification of fats, breaking them into very small micelles, and also activates lipases. Pancreatic lipase then breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
Why: With the duct blocked, fat stays in large globules. Lipase can act only at the surface of a droplet, so digestion is slow, and the undigested fat is passed out in the faeces.
Why not the others: (A) Bile has no digestive enzymes; lipase comes from the pancreas and the intestine. (B) Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase, and trypsin digests proteins, not fats. (C) Gastric secretion does not depend on bile.
Key point: Bile has no enzymes; bile salts emulsify fats for lipase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle from their features
questions.question:
The table compares three muscle tissues.

Tissue | Striations | Control | Cell shape and nuclei | Special feature
P | present | voluntary | long, unbranched, many nuclei | attached to bones
Q | present | involuntary | branched, usually one nucleus | cells joined by intercalated discs
R | absent | involuntary | spindle-shaped, one nucleus | in walls of the gut and blood vessels

Which identification is correct?
options: A) P skeletal, Q cardiac, R smooth
B) P cardiac, Q skeletal, R smooth
C) P skeletal, Q smooth, R cardiac
D) P smooth, Q cardiac, R skeletal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P skeletal, Q cardiac, R smooth.
Concept: Skeletal muscle is striated, voluntary and made of long multinucleate fibres attached to bones. Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary; its branched cells are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which let them contract as a unit. Smooth (visceral) muscle has no striations, is involuntary and has spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus; it lines hollow organs such as the gut and blood vessels.
Why: P has striations, voluntary control and attachment to bones: skeletal. Q is striated, involuntary and has intercalated discs: cardiac. R has no striations and lines the gut and vessels: smooth.
Why not the others: (B) Cardiac muscle is involuntary and has intercalated discs, which describe Q, not P. (C) Smooth muscle has no striations, so it cannot be Q; intercalated discs mark cardiac muscle. (D) Smooth muscle is not voluntary or striated, and skeletal muscle is striated.
Key point: Striated + voluntary = skeletal; striated + involuntary + intercalated discs = cardiac; non-striated = smooth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Dependence of the action potential on sodium ions outside the axon
questions.question: An isolated nerve fibre is kept in a solution in which all the sodium ions outside the fibre are replaced by an ion that cannot pass through the membrane. The potassium concentrations are unchanged. A stimulus is then applied. What is the most likely result?
options: A) A larger action potential, because sodium normally blocks the impulse
B) An action potential of normal size, because the impulse depends only on potassium
C) Little or no action potential, because the rapid depolarisation depends on sodium ions rushing into the fibre, while the resting potential is almost unchanged
D) The resting potential becomes positive at once, because potassium ions rush into the fibre
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Little or no action potential, because the rapid depolarisation depends on sodium ions rushing into the fibre, while the resting potential is almost unchanged.
Concept: At rest the axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, and the inside is negative (polarised). A stimulus opens Na⁺ channels; Na⁺ flows in and the inside becomes positive (depolarisation). This rise is the action potential. Then K⁺ flows out and the resting potential is restored.
Why: With no sodium outside, there is nothing to flow in when the Na⁺ channels open, so the membrane cannot depolarise and no action potential forms. The resting potential depends mainly on K⁺, whose concentrations are unchanged, so it stays nearly the same.
Why not the others: (A) Sodium entry is what makes the impulse; removing sodium cannot make it bigger. (B) The rising phase depends on Na⁺ entry; K⁺ only restores the resting state. (D) At rest K⁺ tends to leave the fibre, not enter it, and its concentrations have not changed.
Key point: Depolarisation = Na⁺ influx; repolarisation = K⁺ efflux.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: How copper-releasing intrauterine devices prevent pregnancy
questions.question: A copper-releasing intrauterine device (such as CuT) is placed in the uterus. Which statement best describes how it acts?
options: A) It releases hormones that stop ovulation
B) The copper ions it releases suppress sperm motility and the ability of sperm to fertilise the ovum
C) It stops the production of sperms in the testes of the partner
D) It blocks the fallopian tubes surgically
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The copper ions it releases suppress sperm motility and the ability of sperm to fertilise the ovum.
Concept: Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are of three kinds: non-medicated (such as Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20). IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus. The copper ions released suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.
Why: The device acts within the female reproductive tract on sperm that arrive there. Its copper ions reduce sperm movement and their ability to fertilise the egg, so fertilisation is unlikely.
Why not the others: (A) That describes hormone-releasing devices or oral pills, not copper-releasing devices. (C) An IUD in the female cannot act on the testes of the partner. (D) Blocking the fallopian tubes is tubectomy, a surgical method.
Key point: Copper IUD: Cu ions reduce sperm motility and fertilising capacity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Standard EMF, standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant of a copper–silver cell
questions.question:
Standard reduction potentials at 298 K are given below.

Couple | E° / V
\(\ce{Cu^2+/Cu}\) | +0.34
\(\ce{Ag+/Ag}\) | +0.80

For the cell \(\ce{Cu(s) | Cu^2+(aq) || Ag+(aq) | Ag(s)}\), what are \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\), \(\Delta_rG^\circ\) for \(\ce{Cu + 2Ag+ -> Cu^2+ + 2Ag}\), and the equilibrium constant K? (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; 2.303RT/F = 0.059 V)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.46 V; −88.8 kJ mol⁻¹; about \(4\times10^{15}\).
Concept: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\). The standard Gibbs energy is \(\Delta_rG^\circ=-nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\), and it is linked to the equilibrium constant by \(\log K=\dfrac{nE^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.059}\) at 298 K.
Why: Silver has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode: \(E^\circ=0.80-0.34=0.46\ \mathrm V\). Two electrons are transferred: \(\Delta_rG^\circ=-2\times96500\times0.46=-88\,780\ \mathrm J\approx-88.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\). \(\log K=\dfrac{2\times0.46}{0.059}=15.6\), so \(K\approx4\times10^{15}\). A negative \(\Delta_rG^\circ\) and a very large K both show that the reaction goes almost to completion.
Why not the others: (B) It adds the two potentials instead of subtracting them. (C) It uses n = 1; one Cu atom gives two electrons. (D) A positive \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) gives a negative \(\Delta_rG^\circ\) and K > 1.
Key point: \(\Delta_rG^\circ=-nFE^\circ=-2.303RT\log K\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ratio of the time for 99.9% completion to the half-life of a first-order reaction
questions.question: For a first-order reaction, about how many half-lives are needed for 99.9% of the reactant to be used up, and does this number depend on the initial concentration?
options: A) About 3 half-lives; it depends on the initial concentration
B) About 5 half-lives; it does not depend on the initial concentration
C) About 10 half-lives; it does not depend on the initial concentration
D) About 10 half-lives, but only when the initial concentration is 1 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 10 half-lives; it does not depend on the initial concentration.
Concept: For a first-order reaction, \(k=\dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]}\) and \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{0.693}{k}\). Both depend only on the fraction of reactant left, not on the initial concentration.
Why: At 99.9% completion, \(\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]}=1000\), so \(t_{99.9\%}=\dfrac{2.303\times3}{k}=\dfrac{6.909}{k}\). Dividing by \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{0.693}{k}\) gives \(\dfrac{6.909}{0.693}\approx10\). Another way: after 10 half-lives the fraction left is \((1/2)^{10}=1/1024\approx0.1\%\). Since k cancels and only a ratio of concentrations appears, the result is the same for any initial concentration.
Why not the others: (A) 3 is \(\log1000\), not the number of half-lives, and first-order times do not depend on \([A]_0\). (B) After 5 half-lives about 3% is still left. (D) The ratio of concentrations, not the starting value, decides the time in first-order kinetics.
Key point: First order: \(t_{99.9\%}\approx10\,t_{1/2}\), independent of \([A]_0\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Composition of brass as a substitutional alloy
questions.question: A sample of brass contains 70.0% copper and 30.0% zinc by mass. The metallic radii are Cu 128 pm and Zn 137 pm. What is the mole fraction of zinc in the alloy, and what kind of alloy is it? (Cu = 63.5, Zn = 65.4)
options: A) 0.30; an interstitial alloy, because zinc atoms fit into the holes of the copper lattice
C) 0.29; an interstitial alloy, because zinc is the minor component
D) 0.29; a substitutional alloy, because the two metallic radii differ by less than about 15%
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.29; a substitutional alloy, because the two metallic radii differ by less than about 15%.
Concept: Alloys are formed by atoms with metallic radii within about 15% of each other; the atoms of one metal replace those of the other in the lattice. Interstitial compounds are formed when small atoms such as H, C or N are trapped in the holes of a metal lattice.
Given: 100 g alloy: 70.0 g Cu, 30.0 g Zn; r(Cu) = 128 pm, r(Zn) = 137 pm.
Formula/Principle: \(n=\dfrac mM;\ x_{\ce{Zn}}=\dfrac{n_{\ce{Zn}}}{n_{\ce{Cu}}+n_{\ce{Zn}}}\)
Step 1: \(n_{\ce{Cu}}=\dfrac{70.0}{63.5}=1.102\ \mathrm{mol};\ n_{\ce{Zn}}=\dfrac{30.0}{65.4}=0.459\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: \(x_{\ce{Zn}}=\dfrac{0.459}{1.561}=0.294\approx0.29\).
Step 3: Radius difference = \(\dfrac{137-128}{128}\times100\approx7\%\), well within 15%.
Why: Zinc atoms are almost the same size as copper atoms, so they take the places of copper atoms in the lattice rather than squeezing into holes.
Why not the others: (A) 0.30 is the mass fraction, and zinc atoms are far too large to fit into interstitial holes. (B) 0.42 is the ratio \(n_{\ce{Zn}}/n_{\ce{Cu}}\), not the mole fraction. (C) Being the minor component does not make an alloy interstitial; the size of the atoms decides it.
Key point: Similar radii (within ~15%) → substitutional alloy; small atoms in holes → interstitial compound.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Geometrical and optical isomers of square planar [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]
questions.question: How many stereoisomers does the square planar complex \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]}\) have, and are any of them optically active?
options: A) None, because the complex is tetrahedral
B) Two geometrical isomers, cis and trans; neither is optically active
C) Three geometrical isomers; one is optically active
D) Two geometrical isomers; the cis isomer is optically active
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Two geometrical isomers, cis and trans; neither is optically active.
Concept: In a square planar complex of the type \(\ce{[MX2L2]}\), the two X ligands can be next to each other (cis) or opposite each other (trans), giving geometrical isomers. Optical isomers need a structure with no plane of symmetry.
Why: In the cis isomer the two Cl ligands are adjacent; in the trans isomer they are opposite. A square planar complex lies in one plane, and that plane is a plane of symmetry, so neither isomer is chiral.
Why not the others: (A) Pt(II) complexes of this type are square planar; a tetrahedral \(\ce{MX2L2}\) would have no geometrical isomers. (C) Only two arrangements are possible for two pairs of identical ligands on a square. (D) The molecular plane is a mirror plane, so the cis isomer is not optically active.
Key point: Square planar \(\ce{MX2L2}\): cis and trans only; no optical isomers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering complexes by spin-only magnetic moment using valence bond theory
questions.question: Arrange the following in decreasing order of spin-only magnetic moment: \(\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}\), \(\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}\), \(\ce{[FeF6]^3-}\), \(\ce{[CoF6]^3-}\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\ce{[FeF6]^3- > [CoF6]^3- > [Fe(CN)6]^3- > [Fe(CN)6]^4-}\).
Concept: In valence bond theory, a strong-field ligand such as \(\ce{CN-}\) forces the 3d electrons to pair, giving an inner-orbital \(d^2sp^3\) complex. A weak-field ligand such as \(\ce{F-}\) does not, giving an outer-orbital \(sp^3d^2\) complex with the most unpaired electrons. \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM.
Why: \(\ce{[FeF6]^3-}\): \(\ce{Fe^3+}\) \(3d^5\), high spin, n = 5 (5.92 BM). \(\ce{[CoF6]^3-}\): \(\ce{Co^3+}\) \(3d^6\), high spin, n = 4 (4.90 BM). \(\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}\): \(3d^5\) paired as far as possible, n = 1 (1.73 BM). \(\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}\): \(\ce{Fe^2+}\) \(3d^6\) fully paired, n = 0.
Why not the others: (A) This is the increasing order. (B) \(\ce{[FeF6]^3-}\) (n = 5) has more unpaired electrons than \(\ce{[CoF6]^3-}\) (n = 4). (C) Low-spin \(\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}\) (n = 1) has fewer unpaired electrons than high-spin \(\ce{[CoF6]^3-}\) (n = 4).
Key point: \(\ce{F-}\) → high spin (outer orbital); \(\ce{CN-}\) → low spin (inner orbital).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Effect of changing concentrations on the rates of SN2 and SN1 reactions
questions.question: Bromomethane reacts with hydroxide ion by the \(S_N2\) mechanism, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by the \(S_N1\) mechanism. Under the starting conditions, each reaction has a rate of \(1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\). In each case the concentration of the alkyl bromide is doubled and the concentration of hydroxide is tripled. What are the new rates?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bromomethane \(6.0\times10^{-4}\); 2-bromo-2-methylpropane \(2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\).
Concept: \(S_N2\) is a one-step reaction in which the nucleophile attacks as the leaving group departs, so rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order). \(S_N1\) has a slow first step in which RX ionises to a carbocation, so rate = k[RX] (first order) and the nucleophile does not appear in the rate law.
Given: initial rate = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ for each; [RX] × 2, [OH⁻] × 3.
Formula/Principle: \(S_N2:\ r\propto[\ce{RX}][\ce{OH-}];\ S_N1:\ r\propto[\ce{RX}]\)
Step 1: Bromomethane: rate × (2 × 3) = 6 → \(6.0\times10^{-4}\).
Step 2: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane: rate × 2 → \(2.0\times10^{-4}\).
Why: The methyl halide is unhindered and reacts by \(S_N2\), so both concentrations count. The tertiary halide forms a stable tertiary carbocation in a slow step that does not involve hydroxide, so only its own concentration counts.
Why not the others: (B) The \(S_N1\) rate does not depend on [OH⁻]. (C) It swaps the two mechanisms. (D) It adds the factors (2 + 3) instead of multiplying them.
Key point: \(S_N2\): rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]; \(S_N1\): rate = k[RX].

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying primary, secondary and tertiary butanols with the Lucas test
questions.question: Three isomeric alcohols X, Y and Z of formula \(\ce{C4H10O}\) are shaken with Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl with anhydrous \(\ce{ZnCl2}\)) at room temperature. X turns cloudy at once, Y turns cloudy after about five minutes, and Z stays clear. Z has an unbranched carbon chain. Which identification and order of reactivity towards Lucas reagent is correct?
options: A) X butan-1-ol, Y butan-2-ol, Z 2-methylpropan-2-ol; reactivity Z > Y > X
B) X 2-methylpropan-2-ol, Y 2-methylpropan-1-ol, Z butan-2-ol; reactivity X > Y > Z
C) X 2-methylpropan-2-ol, Y butan-2-ol, Z butan-1-ol; reactivity X > Y > Z
D) X 2-methylpropan-2-ol, Y butan-2-ol, Z butan-1-ol; reactivity Z > Y > X
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X 2-methylpropan-2-ol, Y butan-2-ol, Z butan-1-ol; reactivity X > Y > Z.
Concept: Lucas reagent converts alcohols into alkyl chlorides, which are insoluble and make the solution cloudy. The reaction goes through a carbocation, so the order of reactivity is 3° > 2° > 1°. Tertiary alcohols give turbidity at once, secondary alcohols within about five minutes, and primary alcohols give no turbidity at room temperature.
Why: X reacts at once, so it is tertiary: the only tertiary \(\ce{C4H10O}\) alcohol is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Y reacts slowly, so it is secondary: butan-2-ol. Z does not react, so it is primary; with an unbranched chain it is butan-1-ol. The order of reactivity follows the stability of the carbocations, X > Y > Z.
Why not the others: (A) It reverses the identities; a primary alcohol does not react at once. (B) 2-Methylpropan-1-ol is primary and would stay clear, and butan-2-ol is secondary and would turn cloudy. (D) The identities are right, but the order of reactivity is reversed.
Key point: Lucas test: 3° at once, 2° in about 5 minutes, 1° no turbidity at room temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Crossed aldol reaction between two different aldehydes with α-hydrogens
questions.question: A mixture of propanal and butanal is treated with dilute NaOH. Ignoring stereoisomers and dehydration, how many different β-hydroxy aldehydes can form, and what is the product formed when the enolate of propanal adds to butanal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4; 3-hydroxy-2-methylhexanal.
Concept: In the aldol reaction, a base removes an α-hydrogen to give an enolate (carbanion), which adds to the carbonyl carbon of another aldehyde molecule. When two different aldehydes that both have α-hydrogens are used, each can act as the donor (enolate) and each as the acceptor, so four products are possible (two self-aldols and two crossed aldols).
Why: Donor/acceptor pairs: propanal/propanal, butanal/butanal, propanal/butanal and butanal/propanal give four products. Propanal enolate \(\ce{CH3-CH^-–CHO}\) adds to the C=O carbon of butanal to give \(\ce{CH3CH2CH2–CH(OH)–CH(CH3)–CHO}\). Numbering from CHO: C-2 carries the methyl group and C-3 the OH, in a six-carbon chain: 3-hydroxy-2-methylhexanal.
Why not the others: (A) Two counts only the self-aldols or only the crossed aldols. (C) 2-Ethyl-3-hydroxypentanal is formed when butanal is the donor and propanal the acceptor. (D) The two crossed products are different compounds, so there are four, not three.
Key point: Two enolisable aldehydes → 4 aldols; the donor's α-carbon becomes C-2 of the product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Lengthening and shortening the carbon chain in the preparation of amines
questions.question: Two preparations are carried out. In route 1, bromoethane is heated with alcoholic KCN, and the product is reduced with \(\ce{LiAlH4}\). In route 2, propanamide is warmed with bromine and aqueous NaOH. The amine formed in each route is isolated. Which amines are formed?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Route 1: propan-1-amine; route 2: ethanamine.
Concept: Replacing a halogen by cyanide adds one carbon atom; reducing the nitrile gives a primary amine: \(\ce{R-X -> R-CN -> R-CH2NH2}\). In the Hoffmann bromamide degradation, an amide with \(\ce{Br2}\) and NaOH gives a primary amine with one carbon atom fewer: \(\ce{RCONH2 -> RNH2}\).
Why: Route 1: \(\ce{CH3CH2Br -> CH3CH2CN -> CH3CH2CH2NH2}\), propan-1-amine (one carbon more than the bromide). Route 2: \(\ce{CH3CH2CONH2 -> CH3CH2NH2}\), ethanamine (one carbon fewer than the amide; the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate).
Why not the others: (B) It swaps the two routes: the nitrile route adds a carbon and the Hoffmann route removes one. (C) Route 2 removes the carbonyl carbon, so it cannot keep three carbons. (D) Route 1 keeps the cyanide carbon, and route 2 shortens the chain rather than lengthening it.
Key point: Nitrile reduction: chain + 1 carbon; Hoffmann bromamide: chain − 1 carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying amylose, amylopectin, glycogen and cellulose from linkage and branching
questions.question:
The table describes four polysaccharides made only of glucose.

Polysaccharide | Glucose form | Main linkage | Branching | Source
P | α | C1–C4 | none | plant storage
Q | α | C1–C4 | C1–C6 branches, less frequent | plant storage
R | α | C1–C4 | C1–C6 branches, more frequent | animal storage
S | β | C1–C4 | none | plant cell wall

Which identification is correct?
options: A) P amylopectin, Q amylose, R glycogen, S cellulose
B) P amylose, Q glycogen, R amylopectin, S cellulose
C) P cellulose, Q amylopectin, R glycogen, S amylose
D) P amylose, Q amylopectin, R glycogen, S cellulose
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P amylose, Q amylopectin, R glycogen, S cellulose.
Concept: Starch has two parts. Amylose is a long unbranched chain of α-D-glucose joined by C1–C4 glycosidic links. Amylopectin is branched: C1–C4 chains with C1–C6 branches. Glycogen, the animal storage polysaccharide, is like amylopectin but more highly branched. Cellulose is a straight chain of β-D-glucose joined by C1–C4 links and is the main component of plant cell walls.
Why: P is unbranched α-glucose from plants: amylose. Q is branched α-glucose from plants: amylopectin. R is more highly branched and stored by animals: glycogen. S is made of β-glucose and forms the cell wall: cellulose.
Why not the others: (A) Amylopectin is branched, so it cannot be P, and amylose is unbranched, so it cannot be Q. (B) Glycogen is the animal storage form, so it is R, not Q. (C) Cellulose is made of β-glucose and is found in cell walls, which describes S, not P.
Key point: Amylose unbranched α; amylopectin branched α; glycogen more branched α (animal); cellulose β.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Moles, molecules and atoms in a given mass of sulfuric acid
questions.question: How many moles of \(\ce{H2SO4}\) are there in 4.9 g of the acid, and how many oxygen atoms does this mass contain? (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32; \(N_A=6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.050 mol; \(1.2\times10^{23}\) oxygen atoms.
Concept: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass; number of molecules = moles × \(N_A\); each molecule of \(\ce{H2SO4}\) contains four oxygen atoms.
Given: m = 4.9 g; M(\(\ce{H2SO4}\)) = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98 g mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: \(n=\dfrac mM;\ N_{\ce{O}}=4nN_A\)
Step 1: \(n=\dfrac{4.9}{98}=0.050\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: Molecules = \(0.050\times6.02\times10^{23}=3.01\times10^{22}\).
Step 3: Oxygen atoms = \(4\times3.01\times10^{22}=1.20\times10^{23}\).
Why: The count of atoms of one element is the number of molecules times the number of those atoms in one molecule.
Why not the others: (A) \(3.0\times10^{22}\) is the number of molecules, not of oxygen atoms. (C) It divides by 9.8 instead of 98. (D) It uses eight oxygen atoms per molecule.
Key point: Atoms of an element = n × \(N_A\) × (atoms per formula unit).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Irregular first ionisation enthalpies down group 13 and poor shielding by d and f electrons
questions.question: The figure shows the first ionisation enthalpies of the group 13 elements B, Al, Ga, In and Tl. Which statement correctly explains the values after aluminium?
options: A) Gallium has fewer electron shells than aluminium, so its value is higher
B) The values fall steadily down the group, exactly as the increasing atomic size predicts
C) Gallium has ten 3d electrons, and thallium has fourteen 4f and ten 5d electrons; these shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the outer electrons are held more strongly than size alone suggests
D) Thallium has a half-filled p subshell, which makes its first electron hard to remove
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Gallium has ten 3d electrons, and thallium has fourteen 4f and ten 5d electrons; these shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the outer electrons are held more strongly than size alone suggests.
Concept: Down a group, ionisation enthalpy usually falls because the atom gets larger and inner electrons shield the outer ones. d and f electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so after they are added the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons is larger than expected.
Why: From the figure, the value falls sharply from B (801 kJ mol⁻¹) to Al (577), but Ga (579) is slightly above Al, and Tl (589) is above In (558). In Ga the ten 3d electrons, and in Tl the 4f and 5d electrons, do not shield the outer 4s/4p and 6s/6p electrons well. The extra effective nuclear charge cancels the effect of the larger size.
Why not the others: (A) Gallium has one more shell than aluminium, not fewer. (B) The values do not fall steadily: Ga is above Al and Tl is above In. (D) Thallium has the outer configuration \(6s^26p^1\); its p subshell holds one electron, not three.
Key point: Poor shielding by d and f electrons raises the ionisation enthalpies of Ga and Tl.
